passage:
Week 1. In Zubin's first meeting as front-office lead at the hotel, he suggested moving check-in to a tablet system. Six heads nodded. Nobody asked a single question. By Friday the system was crashing, and he heard in the corridor that Afreen had seen the problem coming.
Week 2. Zubin thought about it on the bus home. When he was a receptionist, he'd never argued with the old manager either. The title did it. So on Monday he opened the meeting differently: "Before I share my idea, tell me what could go wrong with it. I mean it." Silence, then Afreen spoke up about the weak signal in the lobby.
Week 4. Afreen came to his desk with bad news: a double booking for a wedding party. Zubin said, "Thank you for telling me early," and meant it. Two others brought problems that same week.

qa.q: What did Afreen raise when Zubin asked what could go wrong?
qa.a: Afreen spoke up about the weak signal in the lobby.

qa.q: What did Zubin realise on the bus home?
qa.a: He realised his title made people quiet, just as he had never argued with the old manager when he was a receptionist.

qa.q: Why was thanking Afreen for the double booking news important?
qa.a: Thanking Afreen for bad news showed it was safe to speak up, which is why two others brought problems that same week.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt watching the tablet system crash?
qa.a: Afreen may have felt frustrated and a bit guilty, having seen the problem coming but not feeling able to say so.

grounding: A young lead notices his staff never disagree, realises his title silences them, then invites problems early and thanks bad news.

passage: Anirban, you tell me your team agrees with everything you say. That reminds me of young Tsering, when I worked under him at the tea estate office in Darjeeling. He was twenty-five, the owner's nephew, and every meeting ended in nods. Then one monsoon the drying machine broke, and we all knew it had been making a noise for weeks. Nobody had told him. I still remember his face. He didn't shout. At the next meeting he said, "I'm the owner's nephew, so maybe you're afraid to tell me things. Before I speak, each of you tell me one worry." He started with me. I was so nervous my cup rattled. When I told him about the leaking roof, he said, "Thank you, Dolma-la. This is exactly what I need." After that, we told him everything.

qa.q: What had been making a noise for weeks?
qa.a: The drying machine had been making a noise for weeks.

qa.q: What did Tsering seem to realise after the drying machine broke?
qa.a: He seemed to realise that being the owner's nephew made people afraid to tell him things, so his meetings ended in nods.

qa.q: What could Anirban borrow from Tsering's approach?
qa.a: Anirban could ask each person for one worry before Anirban speaks, and thank whoever brings bad news.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel being asked first for a worry?
qa.a: Dolma was so nervous the cup rattled, but felt valued when Tsering thanked Dolma for the news about the leaking roof.

passage: The school-bus tracking project was due to the client in two days, and the office generator had failed again, so Rajat held the team meeting by the window in the afternoon heat. "Any concerns about the launch?" he asked. Deepika and Farida looked at their notebooks. Silence. It was always silence. Rajat was about to say, "Great, let's go," when he remembered a line from his last job: if nobody disagrees, you haven't heard the truth yet. He was the founder; of course they didn't want to be the one who slowed him down. So he tried again. "I'll go first. My worry is the rural routes. Now each of you, one worry, and I'll thank you for it." Farida hesitated, then said the tracking failed in the hills during testing. Deepika added that two schools hadn't sent route lists. Rajat wrote both down. "Thank you. That's the most useful thing anyone's said all week."

qa.q: What did Farida say failed in the hills during testing?
qa.a: The tracking failed in the hills during testing.

qa.q: Why did Rajat decide the silence wasn't agreement?
qa.a: He remembered that if nobody disagrees you haven't heard the truth yet, and realised that as founder his staff didn't want to slow him down.

qa.q: Why did going first with his own worry help?
qa.a: Naming his own worry first made it safer for others to share theirs, and promising thanks lowered the risk of speaking.

qa.q: What might it be like for Deepika to report the missing route lists?
qa.a: Deepika might feel nervous about delaying the launch, then relieved when Rajat calls it the most useful thing all week. 🙏

passage:
Devesh had been head of the Bengaluru branch of the travel company for six months when he noticed something odd. In every Monday meeting, when he proposed an idea, his team nodded. Himani took notes. Pallavi said, "Good idea, sir." Nobody ever said no.
Then a new holiday package he'd pushed flopped badly. Afterwards, over tea, Pallavi admitted she had seen the problem with the hotel dates in the first week. "I didn't want to contradict you in front of everyone, sir."
That night Devesh realised his title was doing the talking. The next Monday he changed the start of the meeting. "Before I share my view, tell me what could go wrong with this plan. Himani, you first."
Himani hesitated, then listed two risks. Devesh wrote both on the board. "Thank you. That's exactly what I need." When Pallavi brought him a bad review from a customer that week, he thanked her in front of the team.

qa.q: What did Pallavi admit over tea about the holiday package?
qa.a: She admitted she had seen the problem with the hotel dates in the first week.

qa.q: What did Devesh realise after Pallavi's admission?
qa.a: He was troubled to realise that his title was doing the talking, and that people stayed silent because they didn't want to contradict him in front of everyone.

qa.q: What changes did Devesh make to his meetings, and why might they work?
qa.a: He asked for what could go wrong before sharing his view, called on Himani first, and thanked people who brought bad news, so disagreeing felt safe and useful.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when Devesh asked her to go first?
qa.a: Himani probably felt nervous, as the hesitation shows, but also trusted, especially when he wrote the risks on the board and thanked Himani.

grounding: It shows a leader noticing staff never disagree, realising his title silences them, then inviting dissent first and thanking people who bring bad news.

"Sudha, stay a minute after the meeting?"
Sudha stopped at the door of the conference room. "Yes, sir? Is something wrong?"
"No. That's what I want to ask you," Mohit said. "Eight months. Not one person has disagreed with me in a single meeting. Either I'm always right, or something's off."
Sudha smiled nervously. "You're the regional manager, sir."
"So you all just agree?"
"Mostly. It's… easier."
Mohit rubbed his forehead. "That's on me. Here's what I'll try. Next meeting, I'll ask for problems before I say what I think. And if you bring me bad news, I'll thank you. Properly."
Sudha hesitated. "Then… the new delivery schedule. The drivers think it won't work in the rains."
Mohit took out his notebook. "Thank you. Tell me everything."
Sudha let out a breath she seemed to have been holding for months.

qa.q: How long had it been since anyone disagreed with Mohit in a meeting?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What does Sudha letting out a long breath at the end suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she had been holding back worries for a long time and felt relieved that she could finally say them without trouble.

qa.q: What turning point shows Mohit's new approach is working?
qa.a: When Sudha brings up the drivers' worry about the delivery schedule, Mohit takes out his notebook and thanks her, showing that bad news is welcome.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when Sudha finally raises the delivery schedule problem?
qa.a: Mohit is probably relieved and grateful, since eight months of agreement had made him suspect something was off, and he thanks Sudha as promised.

grounding: It shows a leader noticing staff never disagree, recognising his title mutes them, and inviting dissent and thanking bad news.

passage: When I became the youngest branch manager in our company, I was proud that meetings went so smoothly. Every idea I suggested, everyone agreed with. Then in March a project I had pushed failed badly, and afterwards Naveen, our most experienced clerk, said quietly, "Joseph sir, some of us saw it coming." I asked why nobody had said so. He looked at the floor. "You're the manager." That hit me hard. My title was doing the talking and switching everyone else off. So I changed how meetings start. Before I say anything, each person writes one worry on a slip, and we read them out without names. And whenever someone brings me bad news, I thank them out loud, in front of the team. Last week Naveen told me our new form was confusing. I said thank you. He smiled.

qa.q: What does each person write before the manager speaks?
qa.a: One worry on a slip.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Naveen said "You're the manager"?
qa.a: Joseph felt shaken and a bit ashamed, realising the title had been silencing people.

qa.q: What two changes did Joseph make, and why do they work?
qa.a: Anonymous worry slips at the start of meetings and thanking people publicly for bad news, which make disagreement feel safe.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel being thanked for pointing out the confusing form?
qa.a: Naveen probably feels respected and more confident to speak, as his smile suggests.

grounding: A young manager recalls realising his title silenced staff, and how he began inviting worries early and thanking bad news.

passage:
Leadership coach's note, session four with Darshan, 3 June
Darshan, six months into leading the product team, told me today that his meetings had become "too quiet." He had noticed that nobody disagreed with him, even about a launch plan he suspected was weak. He said he used to think this meant he was right. Now he thinks his title is muting people. This week he tried two things we had discussed. He asked for concerns before sharing his own view, and he thanked people publicly for bad news. On Thursday, Zainab from testing told the whole meeting that the launch build was failing on older phones. He thanked her in front of everyone and moved the date. He said it felt uncomfortable, and right. We will review how the team responds next month.

qa.q: What problem did Zainab report?
qa.a: The launch build was failing on older phones.

qa.q: How did thanking Zainab feel for Darshan?
qa.a: It felt uncomfortable and right to him, awkward but in line with the kind of leader he wants to be.

qa.q: What two things did Darshan try, and why do they help?
qa.a: Asking for concerns before giving his own view, and thanking people publicly for bad news, which makes it safer to disagree.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel after being thanked in the meeting?
qa.a: Zainab probably felt relieved and valued, having risked bringing bad news in front of everyone.

grounding: A coach records a young leader noticing his title mutes his team, inviting concerns early and thanking a colleague for bad news.

passage:
Tuesday, after closing
Third week as head chef, and I finally noticed something. When I ask "Any problems?" at the morning briefing, everyone says, "No, chef." Every day. Then at 9 p.m. things go wrong that clearly someone knew about. Today the fridge had been making a noise for four days, and nobody told me until it died.
Gurpreet said to me afterwards, "Chef, people don't want to be the one who brings you bad news." I didn't know I was that scary. I think it's the title, not me. Or both.
Tomorrow I'm changing the briefing. I'll ask, "What's the one thing most likely to go wrong today?" and go round the whole line, starting with the newest. Whoever brings bad news first gets a thank-you on the board.
Tanvir

qa.q: How long had the fridge been making a noise?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What did Tanvir feel on hearing Gurpreet's explanation?
qa.a: Tanvir felt surprised and a little uneasy, not having realised the title made people too scared to speak.

qa.q: How is Tanvir changing the briefing, and why?
qa.a: Asking what is most likely to go wrong, going round the line starting with the newest, and thanking the first bearer of bad news on the board, so speaking up feels safe.

qa.q: How might the newest cook feel being asked first?
qa.a: The newest cook might feel nervous but also taken seriously, with a real chance to speak before the seniors set the tone.

passage: At the cooperative sugar mill in Karad, Vikas had been manager for a year, and every Monday meeting went the same way. He spoke. The supervisors nodded. "Yes, sir." Then things went wrong on Wednesday that someone had surely known about on Monday. This week a boiler valve failed, and the shift lost six hours. Afterwards, in the corridor, he heard Lakshmi, the maintenance clerk, whisper to a colleague, "I told the foreman the valve was leaking. Nobody tells sir bad news." Vikas stood still. So it was him. The next Monday he opened differently. "Before I say anything: what's the worst problem on your floor this week?" Silence. Then Lakshmi raised her hand. "The second valve is leaking too, sir." Vikas thanked her in front of everyone, and sent the fitter out before the meeting ended.

passage:
Amandeep had been head of the hospital's admin department for six months. In every weekly meeting, he'd share a plan, and everyone would nod. No questions. No objections.

At first he thought the plans were good. Then a new billing process he'd pushed failed badly. Afterwards, Anand, one of the clerks, admitted quietly, "We all thought it wouldn't work, sir. Nobody wanted to say."

Amandeep felt a chill. His title was silencing people.

At the next meeting, he tried something new. Before sharing his own view, he asked, "What problems do you see with this idea? I want to hear them first."

Silence. Then Anand spoke, carefully. Then two others.

After the meeting, Amandeep found Anand. "Thank you for speaking up. That's exactly what I need."

Over the next month, he thanked people publicly whenever they brought bad news early. The meetings got louder. And the plans got better.

qa.q: How long had Amandeep been head of the admin department?
qa.a: For six months.

qa.q: What did Amandeep feel when Anand admitted nobody wanted to speak?
qa.a: Amandeep felt a chill of alarm and some shame, realising his title was silencing his staff.

qa.q: What changes did Amandeep make, and why did they work?
qa.a: He asked for problems before sharing his view and thanked people who brought bad news, making disagreement feel safe.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt speaking first at the next meeting?
qa.a: Anand probably felt nervous but encouraged, since Amandeep had invited problems first.

grounding: A department head notices staff never disagree, realises his title mutes them and invites dissent early.

passage:
Dear Francis,

I wanted to share something I've noticed since becoming branch manager, and ask for your help.

In our weekly meetings, nobody disagrees with me. Not once in three months. At first I thought that meant my ideas were good. But last week the new loan-processing plan I'd pushed had three problems that the team clearly saw coming. Nobody mentioned them until it was too late.

I think my title is making people quiet. That worries me.

So from next week I'm going to try something. I'll ask for concerns before I share my own opinion. And whenever someone brings bad news early, I'll thank them in front of everyone.

You've worked here longer than me, and people trust you. Could you help me by being the first to disagree, just for the first few meetings? That might make it feel safer for others.

Thank you,
Santosh

qa.a: Not once in three months.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about the silence in meetings?
qa.a: Santosh feels worried, realising the title may be making people quiet.

qa.q: What does Santosh plan, and why is asking Francis for help clever?
qa.a: Santosh will ask for concerns first and thank bad news publicly; having a trusted colleague disagree first makes it feel safer for others.

qa.a: Francis might feel trusted and a bit amused, and glad to help change the team's habits.

You asked what surprised me most about being a manager, Sarita? I'm Pranav. I'll tell you.

When I got promoted last year, I thought I'd run great meetings. I'd present an idea, everyone would nod, we'd move on. I loved it.

Then a project went wrong. A big one. And after it failed, three people came to me separately and said they'd seen the problem coming months ago.

I asked, "Why didn't you say?"

One said, "You're the manager. We didn't want to seem rude."

That hurt. I realised the nodding wasn't agreement. It was my title shutting people up.

So I changed things. Now I ask for objections before I share my view. I say, "Tell me why this won't work." And when someone brings bad news, I thank them in front of everyone.

At first it was awkward. Now people argue with me all the time. The work is much better.

qa.q: How many people came to Pranav after the project failed?
qa.a: Three people came to me separately.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel on hearing why people stayed silent?
qa.a: Pranav felt hurt, realising the nodding came from fear of the title, not agreement.

qa.q: What did Pranav change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pranav asked for objections before sharing a personal view and thanked bad news publicly, which made dissent safe and improved the work.

qa.q: How might Pranav's team feel now?
qa.a: The team probably feels freer and more valued, since their objections are welcomed.

grounding: A new manager notices staff never disagree, realises the title mutes them and invites dissent early.
